The clinical presentation is classic for acute parvovirus B19 infection (erythema infectiosum): a biphasic rash — initial “slapped-cheek” facial erythema with perioral sparing, followed by a lacy, reticular, generalized rash — occurring in the context of mild, nonspecific prodromal symptoms (low-grade fever, rhinorrhea, headache). The timeline (facial rash beginning 4 days ago, reticular rash emerging over past 2 days) aligns perfectly with the typical evolution of fifth disease. Crucially, features that would suggest key mimics are explicitly absent: no conjunctivitis, cough, or lymphadenopathy (arguing against measles/rubella); no pharyngitis or exudate (against streptococcal scarlatiniform rash); and no systemic toxicity, cytopenias, or organomegaly (against more serious viral exanthems or hematologic disorders). The diagnostic plan appropriately prioritizes parvovirus B19 IgM — the gold-standard serologic test for acute infection — while wisely deferring low-yield tests (e.g., measles/rubella IgM, strep testing) given the high specificity of the clinical picture. - One-week history of low-grade fever, rhinorrhea, and headache (typical prodrome of parvovirus B19).  
- Periorally-sparing facial erythema (“slapped-cheek”) beginning 4 days ago (pathognomonic first phase of erythema infectiosum).  
- Generalized, mildly pruritic, reticular rash on trunk and extremities over past 2 days (characteristic second-phase rash).  
- Absence of conjunctivitis, cough, and lymphadenopathy (reduces likelihood of measles or rubella).  
- Absence of pharyngitis or exudate (reduces likelihood of streptococcal infection).  
- Absence of systemic toxicity, cytopenias, purpura, or hepatomegaly (argues against serious alternative etiologies).  
- Recommended first-line test is serum parvovirus B19 IgM antibody (standard confirmatory test for acute infection).

Acute parvovirus B19 infection
